title: Check a camping stove's connection to its gas cartridge with soapy water, and tighten it if it bubbles
instruction: Check the stove's connection to its cartridge with the soapy water and the brush. If bubbles form, screw the stove down tight and check again. Put the brush back in the pot.
context: Screw-on gas cartridges are the usual fuel for camping stoves. The instruction sheet of the stove modelled here (MSR PocketRocket 2) tells owners to close the flame adjuster, finger-tighten the stove onto the canister, never overtighten it, and to "check for leaks using soapy water", never with a flame: bubbles mean the joint is not tight. The joint is under pressure as soon as the stove is on the cartridge, so the control stays closed throughout, and the free-standing cartridge has to be held or pressed onto the table while the stove is turned, or it turns with the stove. A sound joint and one a third of a turn short look the same; only the test tells them apart, and only a test made after tightening shows that it worked.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y left. A 100 g threaded-valve gas cartridge (90 mm across, 70 mm tall, 200 g), free-standing at x 22, y -8. A folding canister-top stove (MSR PocketRocket 2, 73 g) screwed onto it with its pot supports folded, a column 38.5 mm across whose top is 145 mm above the table; its flame control, a wire handle 45 mm long, is closed. A steel pot 60 mm across and 70 mm tall with 20 mm of soapy water at x 14, y 16. A brush 150 mm long with a 12 mm round head stands in the pot, leaning on its rim, handle towards the arms. By seed the stove is screwed home or a third of a turn (120 degrees) short; the two look the same.
scoring: 0 for the whole trial if the flame control is opened more than 20 degrees, the cartridge is tipped more than 45 degrees or leaves the table, or the stove is unscrewed to 170 degrees from home; also 0 without a valid test. A valid test: at least half of the joint line round the stove's base is wet while the wet brush is on the line (a stretch stays wet for 10 s, the brush for 20 s after it left the water). 0.25 for a valid test; 0.5 if the stove is also within 10 degrees of home at the end; 0.75 if the last valid test came after the stove was last turned on its thread by more than 5 degrees (travel past home does not count: there the stop gives and the thread does not turn); 1.0 if, in addition, the brush is back in the pot and released, both grippers are at least 5 cm clear, and the cartridge stands upright within 3 cm of where it stood. Test and tightening may come in any order; tightening gently first and testing once afterwards is a valid way. Over-tightening is not scored: the cartridge stands free, so the stove can only be tightened with what the hold on the cartridge stands, and a bench has no gauge in the joint.
reset_notes: Wipe the joint and the brush dry, top the pot up, screw the stove home or back it off a third of a turn as the trial requires, flame control closed. Real trials use an EMPTY cartridge pressurised with air to 1 bar through a refill adapter, never fuel gas; witness marks on the stove base, the cartridge and the control spindle; keep soapy water off the gripper pads (wipe between trials) and stand the cartridge in a catch tray.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in PhysX. The thread is a turning joint with 0.05 N m of dry friction and a sprung stop at home (10 N m/rad), without axial travel; it spans 175 degrees where a real stove unscrews over several turns, so "unscrewed" is scored at 170 degrees. A real stop is hard; the spring stands for the give of arm and grip on real hardware, because the simulated arm is stiff. Nothing is scored past home. Two fingertips pressed on the free cartridge hold it against 0.2 N m at 20 N and 0.4 N m at 30 N; forced further, the cartridge turns with the stove. The joint leaks while the stove is more than 30 degrees short of home. Wetting and froth are computed: the brush is wet for 20 s after its bristles were under water, a stretch of the joint line is wet for 10 s after the wet bristles passed within 3 mm of it, and froth is drawn on the cartridge's shoulder beside the wet stretches as white balls 8 to 14 mm across that give off half their white as light of their own, so that they read as white in the stove's shadow. The bristles do not collide with stove or cartridge. The cartridge's rim has a friction of 0.2 on the table. Placeholders for measurements on the trial hardware: the back-off at which a real joint froths steadily, the thread's turning torque and the rim's friction.
